findings.claim: Unconditionally overwriting status and version and removing the version check breaks the accepted rule that projections must not move a shipment back to an older version.
findings.evidence: design.md:7 says to 'overwrite the stored status and version with the event fields' and to 'Remove the existing version check'. adr-004-events.md:3 (accepted, r1) says the broker 'may redeliver and reorder shipment events' and projections 'must not move a shipment back to an older version'. The baseline src/projector.py:3-5 locks the row and returns when event.version <= row.version.
findings.rationale: If version 5 is applied and then a redelivered or late version 4 arrives, the stored row goes back to version 4 with its older status. Support staff then see a stale shipment state, and nothing corrects it until a newer event arrives. Retrying failed messages (design.md:4) and running parallel workers (design.md:7) both make this more likely.

findings.claim: The stated reason for removing the check, that parallelism makes duplicate detection unnecessary, is wrong. The change also drops the atomic per-shipment check-then-act.
findings.evidence: design.md:7: 'parallelism makes duplicate detection unnecessary'. adr-004-events.md:3 says redelivery happens and that shipment_id plus version identify a logical event. src/projector.py:2-3 runs the compare and write inside a transaction holding a row lock.
findings.rationale: Parallel workers on a shared queue do not remove broker redelivery, and they add reordering between workers. Without the transaction and row lock, two workers handling events for the same shipment can interleave. The final state then depends on which write lands last, not on which version is newer, and a duplicated or retried event takes effect again.

findings.claim: Logging the complete HTTP authorization header breaks the accepted ADR and puts credentials in logs that are kept for 14 days.
findings.evidence: design.md:10: 'log the complete received HTTP authorization header together with shipment_id. Retain these logs for 14 days'. adr-004-events.md:3: 'Authentication tokens must never be written to logs.'
findings.rationale: Every failed event writes a full bearer credential to logs. Anyone with log access can read and reuse it for 14 days, and the design itself says retries and failures are expected.

findings.claim: Rolling back by replaying all source events from the beginning, with no ordering or version filter, does not reliably restore correct projections.
findings.evidence: design.md:13: 'roll back by replaying all source events from the beginning; no replay ordering or version filter is required'. adr-004-events.md:3: events may be reordered and redelivered, and projections must not move to an older version. design.md:7 removes the version check.
findings.rationale: With overwrite-on-receive and no version filter, the state after replay is set by whichever event for each shipment is processed last, which may be an older version. So the recovery path can also leave shipments regressed. It replays the new flow's behaviour instead of reverting it, and the design gives no way to confirm the rollback succeeded.

findings.claim: The delivery plan names an undefined component and an undefined done criterion, so it has no concrete scope or acceptance condition.
findings.evidence: design.md:16: 'Make the Flux shim production ready and run verification. Neither Flux shim nor production ready is defined elsewhere in this document.' Neither term appears in adr-004-events.md, README.md or src/projector.py.
findings.rationale: No one can tell what has to be built, what 'verification' covers, or when the work is finished. Nothing links the 3,000 events/s and p99 < 2 s targets (design.md:4) to any acceptance check.

uncertainties: design.md:4 sets a p99 projection lag target below 2 s but alerts only on a 'five-minute lag budget breach'. It is unclear whether five minutes is a separate budget or the alert threshold. If it is the alert threshold, lag that misses the 2 s target by a wide margin would not trigger any alert.

No source shows that the row lock in src/projector.py:3 stops the design from reaching 3,000 events/s. The removal of the version check (design.md:7) seems driven by performance, but no measurement is cited.
design.md:13 enables the new flow for all tenants at once. That widens the impact of any defect, but no source requires a staged rollout, so this is a risk, not a defect.
The 14-day log retention (design.md:10) has no stated lookup or support need to compare against, so whether it is long enough cannot be judged. The token exposure finding applies whatever the window.
src/projector.py:3 assumes lock_row returns an existing row. Behaviour for the first event of a new shipment is not defined in any supplied source.

design.md:7 acknowledges after the overwrite but does not say whether the write and the acknowledgement are atomic. A crash between them causes redelivery, which is only harmless if the version check stays.
